sections.heading: Dialogue II, Knot x (printed pp. 229–235)
rows: [p. 229] [Margin: Nodus 10. motum circularem ex vi sua non eiicere imposita.] Ereu. Prava est mihi memoria; dignaberis itaque permittere ut de hoc primo dicam, & ordine quae tibi visa fuerint, caetera suggeres. Hoc itaque quod quasi inter partes ex consensu accipitur, ego plurimum dubitandum credo.

[p. 229] [Margin: Knot 10. That circular motion out of its own force [vi] does not cast off [eiicere] the things placed upon [it] [imposita].] Ereu. Bad is my memory; you will deign therefore to permit that I speak of this first, and in the order which shall have seemed [good] to you, you will supply [suggeres] the rest. This therefore, which is accepted as if between the parties [partes] by consent, I believe is very much to be doubted.

Video enim in molis tum his quibus ferramenta exacuuntur, tum aliis aquam placide per molae latera decurrere. Et cum mecum perpendo cur motus circularis hunc effectum sortiri habeat, nihil invenio, nisi forte quia quod impositum est rotae, dum in summo est, non elabitur, sed in declivi, ubi [p. 230] fortassis rota quandam pellentis naturam habeat. Vel certe quod asperitate quam in summo habent rotae, apprehendunt imposita, & sic proiiciunt: quod neque ipsum ex natura motus circularis erit, sed potius ex defectu: circularis enim motus qua talis debet in orbem convertere. Propterea suspicor hunc effectum magis ex eo sequi quod rotationibus nostris aliquid motus recti permixtum est.

For I see, in millstones [molis], both in these by which iron tools [ferramenta] are sharpened and in others, water run down gently along the sides of the millstone [molae]. And when I weigh with myself why circular motion should have [habeat] to obtain [sortiri] this effect, I find nothing, unless perhaps because what is placed upon the wheel, while it is at the top, does not slip off, but [it does] on the down-slope [in declivi], where [p. 230] perhaps the wheel may have a certain nature of a thing driving [pellentis]. Or certainly because, by the roughness [asperitate] which the wheels have at the top, they lay hold of [apprehendunt] the things placed [on them], and so project [proiiciunt] [them]: which itself, too, will not be from the nature of circular motion, but rather from a defect: for circular motion as such [qua talis] ought to turn round into a circle [in orbem]. Therefore I suspect this effect follows rather from this, that something of straight motion [motus recti] is mixed in with our rotations.

Asphal. Me accusa, Ereuni, duas enim probationes vel magis exempla adhibet, quae me oportuerat suggessisse. Quorum alterum est ex rotatione situlae aqua vel lapidibus oppletae, quam qui fune rotat sursum deorsumque, sine aquae lapidumve iactura convertit, ut lapides, neque deorsum vergere possint propter vim extrusionis quam ex rotatione percipiunt. Alterum exemplum est ex ludo quodam puerorum qui arundini fissae lapidem inditum post rotationem proiiciunt, non absimili arte illi qua fundibularii utuntur. His ergo exemplis ad confirmationem utitur.

Asphal. Accuse me, Ereunius, for he [Galileo] applies [adhibet] two proofs, or rather examples, which I ought to have supplied [suggessisse]. Of which the one is from the rotation of a bucket [situlae] filled up with water or with stones, which he who rotates [it] up and down by a rope turns round without loss [iactura] of water or stones, so that the stones neither can tend [vergere] downward on account of the force of extrusion [vim extrusionis] which they receive [percipiunt] from the rotation. The other example is from a certain game of boys, who project, after rotation, a stone put into a split reed [arundini fissae], with an art not unlike that which slingers [fundibularii] use. These examples, therefore, he uses for confirmation.

Ereu. Mira res est, quomodo eaedem causae in subiectis inaequaliter dispositis effectorum miram efficiunt varietatem. Haec ipsa exempla mihi adversam fidem faciunt, nullam videlicet esse in motu circulari extrudendi [p. 231] potentiam. Quis enim cum intellexerit situlam a centro repelli, hoc rotationi acceptum referat, cuius natura est aequalitatem ad centrum seu consistentiam facere. Fundae vero vel cannae quamvis primum motum circularem videamus, eundem tamen in rectum converti, cum emittendus est lapis (nisi ego fallor) experimur.

Ereu. A wonderful thing it is, how the same causes, in subjects [subiectis] unequally disposed, effect a wonderful variety of effects. These very examples make for me the opposite belief [adversam fidem]: namely, that there is in circular motion no power [p. 231] [potentiam] of extruding. For who, when he has understood that the bucket is driven back [repelli] from the centre, would credit [acceptum referat] this to rotation, whose nature is to make equality toward the centre, or steadiness [consistentiam]? But of the sling [fundae] or of the cane, although we see the first motion [to be] circular, yet that the same is turned into straight [motion] when the stone is to be let go, we find by experience [experimur] (unless I am deceived).

In primo itaque exemplo si penitus inspiciamus quemdam motum rectum circulari exordium dantem comperiemus, quod, nisi fallor, omni circulari motui qui apud nos frequens est, commune inveniemus: nascitur enim plerumque quasi per compositionem motus recti, qui cum progredi non possit, in se reflectitur. [Margin: Motum circularem ex duobus rectis plerumque esse compositum.] Videmus enim axem vel inter duo recta vel in rotundo foramine clausum; qui vel recte tractus repulsam a terra rotam facit circa se redire, sicut in rotis curruum, & simile est in globulis sphaeroidibus quibus assolemus per lusum. Vel axis cui rota continua est, afflictus lateri cavi in quo volvitur in semet revolvitur quia recta proficisci non potest. Et idem est si extrinsecus contra suum axem fixum urgeatur: semper enim motus in initio rectus est & sine aliqua laxitate, seu spatio ad motum rectum non perficitur rotatio. Nunc subiice quid in Galilaeo sequitur.

In the first example, therefore, if we look in thoroughly, we shall discover a certain straight motion giving the beginning [exordium] to the circular, which, unless I am deceived, we shall find common to every circular motion which is frequent among us: for it is born, for the most part, as it were through a composition [compositionem] of straight motion, which, since it cannot go forward, is bent back [reflectitur] into itself. [Margin: That circular motion is for the most part composed of two straight [motions].] For we see the axle [axem] shut in either between two straight [pieces] or in a round hole; which [axle], either, being drawn straight [recte tractus], makes the wheel, driven back [repulsam] by the ground [a terra], return around itself, as in the wheels of carts — and similar is [the case] in the spheroidal little balls which we are accustomed [assolemus] [to use] in play [per lusum]; or the axle, to which the wheel is joined continuously [continua], being dashed [afflictus] against the side of the hollow in which it rolls, rolls round [revolvitur] upon itself because it cannot proceed straight. And the same is [the case] if from outside it is pressed against its fixed axle: for always the motion in the beginning is straight, and without some looseness [laxitate], or space for straight motion, rotation is not accomplished. Now add [subiice] what follows in Galileo.
Asphal. Accipit motum extrusionis per tan[p. 232]gentem circuli fieri, eo argumento, quod sine angulo fiat.
Asphal. He takes [it] that the motion of extrusion comes about along the tan[p. 232]gent of the circle, by this argument, that it comes about without an angle.

Ereu. [Margin: Proiectionem a motu circulari non esse per tangentem.] At exemplis productis contrarium statuitur: nam ex primo exemplo motum in perpendicularem fieri oporteret: ex secundo vero in lineam quae occurreret, maxime vero ad angulum semirectum, postquam ille potentissimus in proiectis habetur.

Ereu. [Margin: That projection [proiectionem] from circular motion is not along the tangent.] But by the examples brought forward the contrary is established: for from the first example the motion would have to come about along the perpendicular; but from the second, along [whatever] line it might meet [occurreret], and most of all at a half-right angle [angulum semirectum], since that is held [to be] the most powerful in things projected.

Consideranti autem motum circularem, vel acclivem, vel declivem esse, vel insensibiliter distantem a tangente verticali, occurrit ex acclivi motu impetum non acquiri (in nostris rotis) quia potius gravitate in adversam motui partem delabetur missile: sed neque ex eo qui horizontalis est, quoniam ille par est huic motui, quem in curribus & navibus habemus, & iam diximus impetum vel nullum, vel parvum admodum imprimere. In declivi tandem motu contemplor eum in quantum progressivus est, pulsus quodammodo rationem habere posse, & magis terram versus proiecturam missile quam ad tangentem. Vel certe elabi permissurum, cum nullus sit impetus motus circularis extra circulum. Et haec dicta sunto ex pura ratione rotae seu motus circularis.

But to one considering that circular motion is either up-sloping [acclivem] or down-sloping [declivem] or insensibly distant from the vertical tangent, it occurs that from the up-sloping motion impetus is not acquired (in our wheels), because the missile [missile] will rather slip down by heaviness [gravitate] toward the part opposite to the motion; but neither from that which is horizontal, since that is equal [par] to this motion which we have in carts and ships, and [which] we have already said impresses impetus either none or very small. In the down-sloping motion, finally, I contemplate [that] it, in so far as it is progressive [progressivus], can in some way have the nature [rationem] of a driving [pulsus], and [is likely] to project the missile more toward the earth than toward the tangent; or certainly to permit [it] to slip off, since there is no impetus of circular motion outside the circle. And let these things be said [dicta sunto] from the pure nature [ratione] of the wheel, or of circular motion.

si autem quid de facto contingat intueri placeat, puto contingere quae adhaerent rotis vel rotatis diversimodis angulis eis insidere seu affigi, & secundum eos angulos fieri proiectionem. [p. 233] Rursus si de tellure inquiramus: quoniam ea centrum eorum quae super ea feruntur intra viscera continet, omne sedens in ea sic se habere ad eam, sicut quod apud nos plano vehitur, quod videmus nullum persentiscere impetum. Et ex dictis patet, quod tangens angulum non faciat cum circulo potius obstare motui & quietem causare quam e contra: & necessarium esse angulum seu quid obstans a tergo, ut pulsus & eiectio consequi ex motu rotationis valeat.

But if it please [you] to look at what happens in fact [de facto], I think it happens that the things which adhere to wheels or to rotated [bodies] sit upon [insidere] or are fixed to them at angles of diverse kinds, and that the projection [proiectionem] comes about according to those angles. [p. 233] Again, if we inquire about the earth [tellure]: since it contains within its bowels [viscera] the centre of those things which are borne upon it, [I think] that everything sitting [sedens] on it is so related to it as that which among us is carried on a plane [plano], which we see perceives [persentiscere] no impetus. And from what has been said it is evident that the tangent, because it does not make an angle with the circle, rather obstructs motion and causes rest than the contrary [e contra]; and that there is necessary an angle, or something obstructing from behind [a tergo], in order that driving [pulsus] and ejection [eiectio] may be able to follow from the motion of rotation.

Asphal. Sequitur in Galilaeo Geometrica demonstratio quod non possit esse extrusio, ex proportionibus tangentium & secantium. Ostendit enim proportionem tangentis ad secantem esse multiplicem in qualibet ratione data, & semper eo maiorem proportionem esse, quo magis ad contactum acceditur, unde cum virtus proiiciens ad gravitatem quae telluri affigit mobile in determinata sit proportione, evidens fit non posse tantam esse ut faciat grave a tellure recedere, sed haec credo tanta evidentia constare, ut laudari magis quam examinari mereantur.

Asphal. There follows in Galileo a Geometrical demonstration that there cannot be extrusion, from the proportions of tangents and secants. For he shows that the proportion of the tangent to the secant is multiple [multiplicem] in any ratio [ratione] given, and that the proportion is always the greater the more one approaches the contact [contactum]; whence, since the projecting virtue [virtus proiiciens], to the heaviness [gravitatem] which fixes the movable [mobile] to the earth [telluri], is in a determinate proportion, it becomes evident that it cannot be so great as to make the heavy [body] recede from the earth [tellure]. But these things, I believe, stand firm [constare] with such evidence that they deserve to be praised rather than examined.

Ereu. Est ut dicis, si constaret esse intrinsecam rei naturam hanc quam gravitatem appellamus. Alioqui negabit Ptolomaeus ullam supposito telluris motu fore gravitatem. [p. 234] Si enim ex hac quam habemus naturae dispositione accidat, haec quae gravia dicimus deorsum vergere, non ex aliqua inclinatione sibi propria, sed quasi ab aliis pulsa, fiet per motum terrae, ut tali naturae perturbato ordine, nulla supersit gravitatis ratio. Quare si sit aliqua virtus in motu circulari eiiciendi, haec eiecta erunt, ex eo quod vis resistens nulla erit.

Ereu. It is as you say, if it were established [constaret] that this, which we call heaviness [gravitatem], is the intrinsic nature of the thing. Otherwise Ptolemy will deny that, the motion of the earth [telluris] being supposed, there will be any heaviness. [p. 234] For if, from this disposition of nature which we have, it happens that these things which we call heavy tend downward not from some inclination proper to themselves, but as if driven [pulsa] by others, it will come about through the motion of the earth [terrae] that, the order of such a nature being disturbed, no account [ratio] of heaviness remains. Wherefore, if there be some virtue in circular motion of casting off [eiiciendi], these things will be cast off, from this, that the resisting force will be none.
Andab. Recte dicis, si post constitutum mundi ordinem, inciperet haec agitatio; sed si est, simul cum ipso mundo incepit, & per consequens gravitatem expellere non posset.

Andab. You speak rightly, if after the order of the world had been established this agitation [agitatio] were beginning; but if it is, it began together with the world itself, and consequently [per consequens] could not expel heaviness.

Ereu. Tantumdem est dicamus gravitatem tolli atque gravitatem non permitti esse; quomodo & Ptolomaeus locutus est: Castra, arbores, montes disiiciendos. Haec enim per modum suppositionis dicuntur, non assertionis: ut ex eo quod accideret his si essent, videamus haec praeventa ab eadem causa existentiam accipere non potuisse.

Ereu. It is just the same [tantumdem] whether we say heaviness is taken away or that heaviness is not permitted to be; in which way Ptolemy too spoke: that camps, trees, mountains would be scattered [disiiciendos]. For these things are said by way of supposition, not of assertion: so that from that which would happen to these things if they existed [essent], we may see that these things, being forestalled [praeventa] by the same cause, could not have received existence.

Asphal. Male nobiscum agis, Ereuni, qui tantas quaestiones intactas praetermittis. Prius ab impetus ratione tractanda te suffuratus es: Nunc gravitatis quoque indolem quasi longe ostentans in primula luce (nisi ego impediam) nos destituis.

Asphal. You deal badly with us, Ereunius, who pass over such great questions untouched. Before, you stole yourself away [te suffuratus es] from treating the nature [ratione] of impetus; now, as if displaying from afar, in the first little light [in primula luce], the disposition [indolem] of heaviness also, you forsake us (unless I prevent [it]).

Ereu. Memineris, Asphali, te in lecto adhuc [p. 235] esse, anhelante iam ad meridiem sole, me longo fatigatum sermone, superesse adhuc aliquantulum ad praefixum scopum viae; & de utraque hac quaestione librum illum (quem toties commemoravi) de Immortalitate Animae sollicita. Inde saturaberis melius longe quam a me expectare poteris homine brevi & obscuro.

Ereu. Remember, Asphalius, that you are still in bed [p. 235] [lecto], the sun already panting toward midday; that I am wearied by long discourse [sermone]; that there still remains a little way [viae] to the goal [scopum] fixed beforehand; and on both these questions solicit [sollicita] that book (which I have so many times mentioned) On the Immortality of the Soul. From there you will be satisfied [saturaberis] far better than you could expect from me, a man brief and obscure.

Asphal. Memini satis me in strato esse (iudice me) beatissimo in orbe terrarum situ: tum semper, tum nunc maxime, dum his per eum supereffluo deliciis. Tui vero miserendum est qui tanta quiete non gaudes.

Asphal. I remember well enough that I am in bed [strato], (I being judge) the most blessed situation [situ] in the world [orbe terrarum]: both always, and now most of all, while through it I overflow [supereffluo] with these delights. But you are to be pitied, who do not rejoice in such great rest [quiete].

Noveris itaque Galilaeo obiectam duplicem proportionem quae demonstratam multiplicitatem tangentis supra secantem evacuaret; alteram gravium inter se comparatorum quae nunquam finitur, alteram velocitatum vel potius tarditatum quibus a quiete versus motum receditur, in quibus etiam infinita proportio reperiri potest. Respondet Galilaeus proportiones quibus fiunt praedictae diminutiones, recte lineis angulos rectilineos facientibus explicari. Notum autem esse Geometris, angulos quos faciunt circuli cum contingentibus diminutionum aliud genus habere, quod tantae exiguitatis sit, ut hae alterae cum his comparari nequeant. Unde concludit sine Geometria, Philosophiam plane mancam esse.

Know, therefore, that there was objected to Galileo a twofold proportion which would empty out [evacuaret] the demonstrated multiplicity [multiplicitatem] of the tangent above the secant: the one, of heavy [bodies] compared among themselves, which is never ended [finitur]; the other, of the speeds, or rather the slownesses [tarditatum], by which one recedes from rest toward motion, in which also an infinite proportion can be found. Galileo answers that the proportions by which the aforesaid diminutions come about are set forth [explicari] by straight lines making rectilinear angles; but that it is known to Geometers that the angles which circles make with tangents [contingentibus] have another kind of diminutions, which is of such great smallness [exiguitatis] that these others cannot be compared with these. Whence he concludes that without Geometry Philosophy is plainly maimed [mancam]. [End of Knot x; Knot xi begins on p. 236.]

terms: eicio: throw out, expel; reicio: hurl back.
The Ptolemaic objection (Almagest I.7) as put by Galileo, Dialogo II: a rotating earth would hurl off what lies on it.
White's term (already in the glossary) for the tendency Galileo discusses with the bucket and sling examples.
things placed upon / things sitting upon
loads, bodies resting on the surface.
The marginal title reads 'imposita' where the table of knots has 'insidentia'.
Galileo's whirled-bucket example (Dialogo II): water stays in a bucket swung in a vertical circle.
Galileo's comparison of the boys' split-reed game with the sling.
ascending / descending part of the wheel's turn.
Aristotelian 'pulsio' as the cause of projectile motion; kept as in D2 earlier.
Used in three senses here: 'pulsus rationem' (nature), 'gravitatis ratio' (account), 'in qualibet ratione data' (mathematical ratio).
tangent line; secant line (here = the segment from the tangent to the circle); point of contact.
Galileo's demonstration (Dialogo II) that near the contact point the tangent exceeds the descent to the circle in every ratio, so no finite projecting impetus can overcome heaviness.
a ratio n:1; here 'in any given ratio' = unbounded.
Sixteenth-/seventeenth-century ballistics (Tartaglia) held 45° gave the greatest range.
by way of supposition / of assertion
Scholastic logic: reading Ptolemy's argument as a reductio, not a factual claim.
Things that would be flung off could never have come to be.
Rare deponent use of suffuror; reproach that Ereunius dodged the impetus question earlier.
at first dawn; at a first glimpse.
Diminutive; the nature of heaviness glimpsed only from afar.
book On the Immortality of the Soul
Digby's Two Treatises (1644), known to White in manuscript; already cited in Dialogue I.
concise and unclear / humble and unknown.
Allusion to Horace, Ars Poetica 25–26, 'brevis esse laboro, obscurus fio'; a self-deprecating pun.
The dialogue's morning setting: Asphalius talks from bed.
Galileo's reply via the horn angle prepares Knot xi.
Galileo's claim that philosophy without geometry is crippled; Ereunius replies in Knot xi that geometers need logic.
notes: Unit: Dialogue II, Knot x, complete in one unit. PDF pp. 240–246 = printed pp. 229–235, from ‘Ereu. Prava est mihi memoria’ (p. 229, beside the margin ‘Nodus 10’) to Asphalius’ ‘…Philosophiam plane mancam esse.’ (p. 235). Knot xi begins on p. 236 (PDF 247) with ‘Ereu. Doctissima prorsus & subtilissima est haec dissertatio’ beside the margin ‘Nodus XI. Angulum contingentiae non esse quolibet rectilineo minorem’.

Offset +11 holds (running heads 229–235; signatures Ff iij p. 229, Gg p. 233, Gg ij p. 235). Marginal notes: p. 229 (knot title, reading ‘imposita’ where the table of knots has ‘insidentia’), p. 231 ‘Motum circularem ex duobus rectis plerumque esse compositum’, p. 232 ‘Proiectionem a motu circulari non esse per tangentem’.

Uncertain or difficult readings: (1) p. 230 printed ‘litulae’/‘ſitulae’: read situlae (bucket), the long s resembling l. (2) p. 230 ‘ut lapides, neque deorsum vergere possint’: ‘neque’ without a matching second term; translated literally. (3) p. 231 ‘quibus assolemus per lusum’: the verb of use (uti/ludere) is not expressed; supplied in brackets. (4) p. 232 ‘proiecturam missile’: feminine form does not agree with ‘eum’ (motum); probably a misprint for ‘proiecturum’, translated as such. (5) p. 233 ‘omne sedens … se habere’: accusative-and-infinitive with no governing verb; ‘[I think]’ supplied from ‘puto’ before. (6) p. 235 ‘per eum’: antecedent unclear (situs? the sun?); rendered ‘through it’.
Subject of ‘adhibet’ and ‘utitur’ in Asphalius’ speech (p. 230) and of ‘Accipit’ (p. 231) is Galileo, unnamed; supplied in brackets.

Verification pass: each Latin sentence was re-read against the page images (with a 300-dpi zoom of the knot margin on p. 229 and of the lower half of p. 235) and against the English, checking omissions, cases, tenses, moods, negatives and comparatives. 1 correction: ‘dicta sunto’ had been padded to ‘let these things be [taken as] said’; restored to the literal ‘let these things be said’. Confirmed on the zoom: margin ‘eiicere imposita’ (p. 229), ‘multiplicitatem’, ‘cum contingentibus’, ‘exiguitatis’ (p. 235). Still debatable: ‘ad praefixum scopum viae’ (viae taken with aliquantulum, ‘a little way’; it could go with scopum, ‘the fixed goal of the journey’).

Conventions as in the glossary: long s → s, æ → ae, macrons expanded (proportionē → proportionem, multiplicitatē → multiplicitatem, cū → cum); u/v normalised as in earlier units; words supplied for sense in square brackets.
